title: Power to Your Home
blurb: You press a switch and the light comes on. But how does electricity travel from a power station to your room?

chapters.title: What Is Electricity?
chapters.text:
Everything around us is made of tiny particles called atoms. A single grain of salt holds more atoms than you could count in a lifetime. Inside atoms there are even smaller particles called electrons, which carry a negative electric charge. In some materials, such as copper, electrons can move easily from one atom to the next. We call these materials conductors.

When a large number of electrons flow in the same direction through a wire, we say that an electric current is flowing. Electric current is not something that you can see, but you can see what it does: it lights a bulb, spins a fan or heats a kettle.

Here is a puzzle. Electrons creep along a wire very slowly, often more slowly than a snail. So how can a lamp come on the moment you press the switch?

Think of a long tube packed full of marbles. Push one marble in at one end, and straight away another marble drops out at the other end. No marble has travelled far, but the push has gone all the way along. A wire works in a similar way. It is already full of electrons, and the push travels along it at a huge speed, close to the speed of light.

Materials such as plastic, rubber and glass hold their electrons tightly. They are called insulators, and they do not let current pass. That is why electric wires have a plastic coat. The metal inside carries the current, and the plastic keeps you safe.

Your body is neither a very good conductor nor a very good insulator, but it can carry a current. A strong current through the body can burn you and can stop your heart. So electricity needs to be respected, even though it is hard to see. A wire with a damaged coat may look harmless, but it is no longer safe.

You can see electrons at work on a small scale. Rub a balloon on dry hair and it picks up extra electrons. Then it can pull your hair towards it, or stick to a wall for a while. Lightning comes from a similar build-up of charge, but on an enormous scale.

questions.prompt: What are the tiny particles with a negative charge called?
options: Atoms
Electrons
Insulators
Conductors
questions.why: Inside atoms there are even smaller particles called electrons, which carry a negative electric charge.

questions.prompt: What do we call materials that let electrons move easily?
options: Currents
Magnets
Insulators
Conductors
questions.why: In materials such as copper, electrons can move easily. We call these materials conductors.

questions.prompt: What is an electric current?
options: A small particle that is found inside every atom
A plastic coat that keeps the metal in a wire safe
A large number of electrons flowing in the same direction
A strong magnet that is pushing against a copper wire
questions.why: When a large number of electrons flow in the same direction through a wire, an electric current is flowing.

questions.prompt: Why does the text describe a tube full of marbles?
options: To explain how a lamp can light at once although electrons are slow
To show how much electricity a single lamp will use up
To explain why copper wire has to be covered in plastic
To show that electrons are about the same size as small marbles
questions.why: No marble travels far, but the push goes all the way along. In the same way, the push moves quickly along the wire, even though electrons creep.

questions.prompt: How fast do electrons themselves move along a wire?
options: At a huge speed, close to the speed of light
At a steady speed of one metre every second
As fast as a car on a very busy road
Very slowly, often more slowly than a snail
questions.why: Electrons creep along a wire very slowly, often more slowly than a snail. It is the push that travels near the speed of light.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an insulator?
options: A metal wire
Copper
Rubber
Lightning
questions.why: Materials such as plastic, rubber and glass are called insulators.

questions.prompt: Why is a wire with a damaged coat no longer safe?
options: The metal that carries current is exposed, and your body can carry current
The plastic coat is what makes the current flow along inside the wire
The wire becomes an insulator, and insulators can burn your hand
The damage will stop the electrons from moving through the metal at all
questions.why: The metal carries the current and the plastic keeps you safe. Without the coat, a body touching the metal could carry a current.

questions.prompt: What happens when you rub a balloon on dry hair?
options: It turns into a conductor and can light a very small bulb
It picks up extra electrons and can pull your hair towards it
It loses all of its atoms and slowly becomes much smaller
It makes a strong current flow through the hair to the floor
questions.why: Rub a balloon on dry hair and it picks up extra electrons. Then it can pull your hair towards it.

chapters.title: Making Electricity
chapters.text:
In 1831, a scientist called Michael Faraday made a discovery on a workbench in London. As a boy, Faraday had very little schooling. He worked for a bookbinder, and he read the science books that he was binding. Years later, he pushed a magnet into a coil of copper wire and watched a needle on a measuring instrument. The needle twitched. A current had begun to flow, and there was no battery anywhere in the circuit.

Almost all the electricity we use today comes from that same idea. In a power station, electricity is made by a machine called a generator. A generator contains a strong magnet and a coil of copper wire. When the magnet spins next to the coil, it pushes the electrons in the wire and a current begins to flow. A small dynamo that lights a bicycle lamp works in the same way.

Something must spin the magnet. Usually, it is a turbine, which is a wheel with blades like a very large fan. In many power stations, steam turns the turbine. The steam is made by boiling water with heat from burning coal or gas. In Indonesia, more than half of all electricity still comes from burning coal.

Other power stations find different ways to turn the same kind of wheel. In a hydroelectric station, falling water spins the turbine. At Cirata in West Java, water from a huge reservoir does this job. In a wind farm, the wind does it. At Sidrap, in South Sulawesi, thirty tall wind turbines stand together in Indonesia's first large wind farm.

In a geothermal power station, steam comes from hot rocks deep underground. Engineers drill wells and let the steam rise up through pipes. Indonesia has many volcanoes, so it has a lot of hot rock, and geothermal energy is an important source there. Kamojang, in West Java, was the country's first geothermal power station, and it is still running.

So however different they look, most power stations are doing the same simple thing as Faraday did on his workbench. They move a magnet and a coil of wire past each other, and they find something strong enough to keep them moving, day and night.

questions.prompt: What did Faraday see when he pushed a magnet into a coil of wire?
options: The magnet stuck to the end of the coil
A small lamp lit up on the bench
The copper wire grew hot and melted
A needle on an instrument twitched
questions.why: He pushed a magnet into a coil of copper wire and watched a needle. The needle twitched.

questions.prompt: How did the young Faraday learn about science?
options: By going to a very expensive school
By asking questions in a science class
By reading the books he was binding
By working in a large power station
questions.why: He worked for a bookbinder, and he read the science books that he was binding.

questions.prompt: Why was it surprising that a current began to flow on Faraday's bench?
options: There was no copper wire anywhere on the bench
There was no battery anywhere in the circuit
The magnet was much too weak to lift a needle
Nobody in London had ever seen a magnet before
questions.why: The text stresses that a current had begun to flow, "and there was no battery anywhere in the circuit". The magnet alone had caused it.

questions.prompt: What are the two main parts of a generator, according to the text?
options: A strong magnet and a coil of copper wire
A boiler and a pipe full of steam
A battery and a long rubber insulator
A large fan and a tall steel tower
questions.why: A generator contains a strong magnet and a coil of copper wire.

questions.prompt: What is a turbine?
options: A wheel with blades like a very large fan
A pipe that carries steam from hot rocks
A strong magnet inside a coil of wire
A tower that carries cables across the land
questions.why: Usually, it is a turbine, which is a wheel with blades like a very large fan.

questions.prompt: What spins the turbine at Cirata?
options: Steam from burning coal
Steam from hot rocks
Wind blowing over the hills
Water from a huge reservoir
questions.why: In a hydroelectric station, falling water spins the turbine. At Cirata, water from a huge reservoir does this job.

questions.prompt: Why is geothermal energy important in Indonesia?
options: It has no coal of its own to burn in power stations
It has many volcanoes, so there is a lot of hot rock
It has too few hills on which to build wind farms
It has very little rain, so its rivers are often dry
questions.why: Indonesia has many volcanoes, so it has a lot of hot rock, and geothermal energy is an important source there.

questions.prompt: What do coal, water, wind and geothermal power stations have in common?
options: Each of them can only be built close to the sea or a river
Each stores its electricity in very large batteries for later
Each finds a way to turn a turbine and move a magnet past a coil
Each burns a fuel, and each makes a lot of smoke and ash
questions.why: Steam, falling water or wind turns the wheel in each case. The last paragraph says they are all doing the same simple thing as Faraday.

chapters.title: Up the Wires
chapters.text:
After the electricity is made, it must travel to towns and cities that may be hundreds of kilometres away. It travels along thick metal cables carried by tall steel towers. There is a problem, however. As current flows through a long wire, some of the energy turns into heat and is lost. The bigger the current, the more energy is wasted.

Engineers solve the problem with a clever machine called a transformer. A transformer has two coils of wire wound around an iron core. A step-up transformer at the power station raises the voltage to a very high level, such as one hundred and fifty thousand volts. You can think of voltage as the push behind the current. When the voltage is high, the current needed to carry the same power is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat. The main lines across Java work at an even higher level, five hundred thousand volts.

If you look up at a tower, you will see stacks of glass or ceramic discs holding up the cables. These discs are insulators. High cables usually have no plastic coat, because the air around them does not easily let current pass. The discs stop the current from reaching the steel tower and running down it to the ground.

All of these cables are joined into a huge network called a grid. Running a grid is a difficult balancing act. Electricity is hard to store in large amounts, so power stations must make about as much as people are using at each moment. In Indonesia, use rises in the early evening, when millions of families turn on their lights and televisions. Engineers in control rooms watch the numbers and bring more generators into action.

Sometimes things go wrong. In August 2019, a fault on the lines left Jakarta and much of western Java without power for many hours. Trains stopped, and traffic lights went dark.

Very high voltage is dangerous, and this is why we see warning signs on tall towers. Nobody should climb near the cables. It is also unsafe to fly a kite close to power lines, because a damp string can carry current down to the person holding it.

questions.prompt: On a very hot evening, millions of people switch on fans and air conditioners. What must the engineers in the control rooms do?
options: Turn off all the step-up transformers
Stop the turbines until it is cooler
Lower the cables closer to the ground
Bring more generators into action
questions.why: Power stations must make about as much as people are using at each moment. When use rises, engineers bring more generators into action.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with sending current along long wires?
options: The current becomes too cold to be used at home
Some of the energy turns into heat and is lost
The wires become too heavy for towers to hold up
The electrons stop moving after a few kilometres
questions.why: As current flows through a long wire, some of the energy turns into heat and is lost.

questions.prompt: What does a step-up transformer do?
options: It raises the voltage to a very high level
It lowers the voltage to a very safe level
It spins the magnet inside the generator
It stores the extra energy for the evening
questions.why: A step-up transformer at the power station raises the voltage to a very high level.

questions.prompt: Why is very high voltage used for long distances?
options: It makes the electrons travel a lot faster along the wire
It is much safer for anyone who lives near the towers
The current needed is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat
It lets engineers use thinner towers that are cheaper
questions.why: When the voltage is high, the current needed to carry the same power is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat.

questions.prompt: What are the stacks of discs on a tower for?
options: They store electricity for use in the evening
They raise the voltage in the high cables
They stop current from reaching the steel tower
They keep birds away from the top of the tower
questions.why: These discs are insulators. They stop the current from reaching the steel tower and running down it to the ground.

questions.prompt: Why can high cables manage without a plastic coat?
options: They are made of a metal that cannot carry any current
They carry too little current to be a danger
They are kept safe by the rain that washes them
The air around them does not easily let current pass
questions.why: High cables usually have no plastic coat, because the air around them does not easily let current pass.

questions.prompt: Why must power stations make about as much electricity as people are using?
options: Electricity is hard to store in large amounts
Families pay for only what they use in the evening
Electricity is too dangerous to send at night
Generators will break if they run all day
questions.why: Electricity is hard to store in large amounts, so power stations must make about as much as people are using at each moment.

questions.prompt: Why is it unsafe to fly a kite close to power lines?
options: The kite could turn the towers and damage the steel
A damp string can carry current to the person holding it
The power lines would pull the kite up into the sky
The wind around power lines is much too strong for a kite
questions.why: The text says a damp string can carry current down to the person holding it.

chapters.title: Cities and Substations
chapters.text:
Before electricity can be used at home, the voltage must come down again. Near the city, the cables enter a substation, which is a fenced area with large machines. Here, step-down transformers lower the voltage in stages. If you walk past one, you may hear a low, steady hum, which comes from the iron core of the transformers shaking very slightly. Substations are never places to play. If a ball goes over the fence, leave it there and tell an adult.

The electricity then runs along smaller cables and wires on poles along the street. In the middle of some big cities, the cables run underground instead. Near your house, a last small transformer reduces the voltage to about two hundred and thirty volts, which is the voltage used in homes in Indonesia. You may be able to see this transformer, which often looks like a large grey box on a pole.

Not every country uses the same voltage. Homes in Japan, for example, use about one hundred volts. A hairdryer made for Japan could burn out if someone plugged it straight into a wall socket in Indonesia.

Islands need special solutions, and Indonesia has more than seventeen thousand of them. In places where islands are close to each other, cables are laid on the sea floor to carry electricity across the water. For example, there is an undersea cable between Java and Bali. A special ship lets the heavy cable slide slowly down to the seabed. Ships' anchors can damage it, so it is marked on sea charts.

Many other islands are too far apart to be joined in this way, so they have their own separate networks. In remote villages without a cable, solar panels or small generators supply power. A small diesel generator needs fuel, and the fuel has to come by boat, so its power can be very expensive. In some hill villages, a small stream turns a tiny turbine, and the people of the village look after it together. These small schemes may only light a few dozen homes, but for a child who can now read after dark, that makes a very big difference.

questions.prompt: What is a substation?
options: A fenced area with large machines that lower the voltage
A station where diesel fuel is brought in by boat
A shop where families can pay for their electricity
A tall steel tower that holds up long metal cables
questions.why: A substation is a fenced area with large machines. Here, step-down transformers lower the voltage in stages.

questions.prompt: What causes the low hum near a substation?
options: Electrons hitting the fence around the large machines
Wind blowing across the cables above the machines
The iron core of the transformers shaking very slightly
Water running through the pipes under the ground
questions.why: You may hear a low, steady hum, which comes from the iron core of the transformers shaking very slightly.

questions.prompt: What should you do if a ball goes over a substation fence?
options: Climb over quickly and fetch it
Ask a friend to help you get it
Use a long stick to reach it
Leave it there and tell an adult
questions.why: If a ball goes over the fence, leave it there and tell an adult.

questions.prompt: About what voltage is used in homes in Indonesia, according to the text?
options: One hundred volts
Two hundred and thirty volts
One hundred and fifty thousand volts
Five hundred thousand volts
questions.why: A last small transformer reduces the voltage to about two hundred and thirty volts, which is the voltage used in homes in Indonesia.

questions.prompt: Why could a hairdryer made for Japan burn out in Indonesia?
options: Indonesian wall sockets supply a much higher voltage than it was made for
The air in Indonesia is too warm for it to cool down after use
Indonesian wall sockets supply much less current than it needs to work
The plugs in Japan are too large to fit into Indonesian sockets
questions.why: Homes in Japan use about one hundred volts and homes in Indonesia use about two hundred and thirty, more than twice as much.

questions.prompt: How can electricity cross the sea between close islands?
options: Through long poles standing in the water
As radio waves sent across the sea
In batteries carried by small boats
Through cables laid on the sea floor
questions.why: Cables are laid on the sea floor to carry electricity across the water.

questions.prompt: Why is power from a small diesel generator often so expensive?
options: It can only be run for a few hours each year
Its fuel has to be brought to the village by boat
It has to be repaired by engineers from Japan
Its turbine needs a very large stream to turn it
questions.why: A small diesel generator needs fuel, and the fuel has to come by boat, so its power can be very expensive.

questions.prompt: What does the last sentence suggest about electricity in a remote village?
options: Solar panels are not able to light a whole home
Only big power stations are worth building at all
Even a small supply can change a child's life
Children in remote villages do not like reading
questions.why: The text says these small schemes may light only a few dozen homes, but a child who can now read after dark gains a great deal.

chapters.title: Inside Your Home
chapters.text:
The electricity enters your home through a meter, which measures how much you use, and then goes to a box with switches called circuit breakers. From there, wires run inside the walls to sockets and lights. Many homes in Indonesia have a prepaid meter. The family buys a long number, called a token, and types it in. When the credit runs low, the meter starts to beep, and someone has to hurry out and buy more.

For a lamp to work, the current must have a complete path, called a circuit. It leaves the supply, passes through the lamp and returns. When you press a switch, you open or close a gap in the circuit. A closed circuit lets current flow, and an open circuit stops it.

The idea of a complete path explains something you may have seen. Birds can sit safely on a single power line. The current has no reason to go through the bird, because the bird does not give it a path to anywhere else. A person standing on the ground and touching a live wire is in a very different position. The body now makes a path from the wire down to the ground, and the current can flow through it. So never try to rescue a kite or a ball from a power line.

Some things use far more electricity than others. A lamp uses very little, but things that make heat, such as a rice cooker or an iron, use a lot. Too many of these on one socket can make the wires dangerously hot.

Circuit breakers keep you safe. If too much current flows, perhaps because a wire has been damaged or a socket is overloaded, the breaker switches itself off and cuts the circuit. Without it, the wires could overheat and start a fire. If a breaker keeps switching off, it is telling you that something is wrong, so ask an adult to get it checked.

Remember these safety rules: never put anything but a plug into a socket, keep water away from sockets, and never touch a damaged wire.

questions.prompt: What does the meter do?
options: It switches on the lights in the evening
It measures how much electricity you use
It makes electricity for the whole house
It stores electricity for use at night
questions.why: The electricity enters your home through a meter, which measures how much you use.

questions.prompt: What does a beeping prepaid meter tell a family?
options: An adult should go outside and check the transformer
The voltage has risen too high, and they should leave
A wire has been damaged, and the circuit is broken
The credit is running low, and they need to buy more
questions.why: When the credit runs low, the meter starts to beep, and someone has to hurry out and buy more.

questions.prompt: What is a circuit?
options: A complete path for the current
A box that measures electricity
A long number typed into a meter
A switch that turns itself off
questions.why: For a lamp to work, the current must have a complete path, called a circuit.

questions.prompt: What happens to a lamp when a switch opens the circuit?
options: The current goes round the house through other wires
The current goes back to the power station at once
The current stops, and the lamp goes out
The current flows faster, and the lamp grows brighter
questions.why: An open circuit stops the current, and a lamp needs current flowing through it to work.

questions.prompt: Why can a bird sit safely on a single power line?
options: The bird gives the current no path to anywhere else
The power line carries no current at all during the day
The bird's feet have a plastic coat that protects them
The bird's feathers are very good conductors of current
questions.why: The current has no reason to go through the bird, because the bird does not give it a path to anywhere else.

questions.prompt: Why is a person on the ground in danger when touching a live wire, although a bird is not?
options: The person is a better insulator than a small bird is
The person's hands are wet, but a bird's feet are always dry
The person's body makes a path from the wire to the ground
The person is much heavier than a bird and pulls the wire down
questions.why: The body now makes a path from the wire down to the ground, so the current can flow through it.

questions.prompt: Why are too many heating things on one socket a risk?
options: They can make the meter run out of its token
They can make the lamps in the house too bright
They can make the current flow in the wrong direction
They can make the wires dangerously hot
questions.why: Things that make heat use a lot, and too many of these on one socket can make the wires dangerously hot.

questions.prompt: What does it probably mean if a breaker keeps switching off?
options: The breaker likes to be reset by whoever is nearest to it
There is a fault, so it needs to be checked by an adult
The family has bought too many tokens for the meter
The house is using too little electricity on that circuit
questions.why: The text says that if a breaker keeps switching off, it is telling you that something is wrong, so ask an adult to get it checked.

chapters.title: Power for Tomorrow
chapters.text:
Today, many power stations burn coal and gas, which release carbon dioxide. This gas traps heat in the air and contributes to climate change. So scientists and engineers are looking for cleaner ways to make electricity.

Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. They have no turbine and no magnet. Instead, sunlight knocks electrons loose in a thin layer of a material called silicon, and a current begins to flow. They are very useful in sunny countries like Indonesia, and they can be placed on roofs. They can even float. On the Cirata reservoir in West Java, a huge field of solar panels has been floating on the water since 2023. The water helps to keep the panels cool, and panels work better when they are not too hot.

Wind turbines and hydro stations make power without burning fuel. Geothermal power stations use the Earth's own heat.

Most of these have a weakness. The sun goes down in the early evening, just when many homes need the most power. The wind can drop for days. In a long dry season, reservoirs run low. A big dam can also flood a valley where people used to live. So engineers mix different sources together, and they are building very large batteries to store power for later. No single answer solves everything, which is what makes this such an interesting problem.

But the cleanest energy of all is the energy that we do not use. Switching off lights when you leave a room, choosing efficient bulbs and unplugging chargers all help. A modern bulb called an LED gives the same light as an old filament bulb for a small part of the energy. In many homes, the air conditioner uses more power than anything else, so setting it a little warmer saves a surprising amount. If every family saved a little, the power stations would have to burn less fuel, and the air would be cleaner for everyone.

The people who solve these problems will need to know about magnets, turbines, grids and much more. Some of them are probably at primary school today. If you have read this far, one of them could be you.

questions.prompt: Which gas is released when power stations burn coal and gas?
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Helium
Nitrogen
questions.why: Many power stations burn coal and gas, which release carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: How is a solar panel different from most other power stations in this book?
options: It burns a small amount of coal
It needs falling water to work
It has no turbine and no magnet
It only works in very cold places
questions.why: Solar panels have no turbine and no magnet. Instead, sunlight knocks electrons loose in a thin layer of silicon.

questions.prompt: Why does floating on water help the panels at Cirata?
options: The water reflects moonlight, so they work through the night
The water turns the panels around to follow the sun
The water carries the electricity to the nearest town
The water keeps them cool, and they work better that way
questions.why: The water helps to keep the panels cool, and panels work better when they are not too hot.

questions.prompt: Why is the time of sunset a problem for solar power?
options: The sun goes down just when many homes need the most power
The grid is switched off in the early evening for repairs
The panels get too hot in the evening and have to rest
The electrons in the silicon fall asleep once it gets dark
questions.why: The sun goes down in the early evening, just when many homes need the most power.

questions.prompt: Why do engineers mix different energy sources?
options: Every source is much cheaper when it is used with coal
Every source is required by a law in every country
A weakness in one source can be covered by the others
Every source works only on one day of the week
questions.why: The text lists weaknesses of the sun, the wind and reservoirs, then says engineers mix different sources together.

questions.prompt: What does the writer call the cleanest energy of all?
options: The energy from the wind
The energy that we do not use
The energy from the sun
The energy from hot rocks
questions.why: The cleanest energy of all is the energy that we do not use.

questions.prompt: In many homes, which change would probably save the most electricity?
options: Switching off one small lamp for an hour
Opening the fridge door a little more often
Unplugging a phone charger once a week
Setting the air conditioner a little warmer
questions.why: The text says that in many homes, the air conditioner uses more power than anything else, and setting it warmer saves a surprising amount.

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the final chapter?
options: We can make and use electricity in cleaner and smarter ways
Only engineers can do anything to help save energy
Electricity is too dangerous for families to use at home
Solar panels have solved every problem with power
questions.why: The chapter describes cleaner sources and their weaknesses, along with ways in which everyone can use less energy.
